title: Aswang Hours
cultural_note: The aswang is a shape-shifter in Philippine folklore, often said to pass as an ordinary neighbor by day. Salt and garlic are among the traditional protections.
short_description: Run a night-shift sari-sari store while something outside counts your customers.
description: You inherited a corner store in a barrio that goes quiet after ten. Serve the regulars, read what they leave unsaid, and decide who gets the last pack of salt before midnight. Every customer might be exactly who they say they are.
highlights: Eight nights, each with its own set of regulars
Folk remedies and warding rituals you can actually use
Local co-op: one person tends the store, one watches the street

title: Tikbalang Crossing
cultural_note: The tikbalang is a tall, horse-headed creature said to lead travelers astray in the mountains. Folk belief says wearing your shirt inside out breaks its spell.
short_description: Lost on a mountain trail? Turn your shirt inside out and bargain with the horse-headed trickster.
description: A turn-based RPG across a trail that rearranges itself. Wear your shirt inside out to keep your bearings, trade riddles for directions, and build a party of travellers who each remember the mountain differently.
highlights: Riddle-and-bargain combat instead of pure damage races
A trail that reshuffles every run
Voiced in Tagalog, Cebuano, and Ilocano with English subtitles

title: Maiba-Taya
cultural_note: Maiba-taya is a street tag game where whoever is tagged becomes the new taya, or 'it'. It is played in neighborhoods and schoolyards across the country.
short_description: Tag the way you played it after class: one taya, one street, and nobody sits out.
description: Online tag for up to eight players. The taya changes with every touch, safe spots shrink as the round goes, and the street map is built from real barrio layouts submitted by players.
highlights: Rounds of two to four minutes
Up to eight players online or against bots
Player-submitted street maps

title: Tumbang Preso
cultural_note: Tumbang preso is a street game where players throw slippers to knock a can off its spot while the taya guards it. It is played in neighborhoods all over the country.
short_description: Guard the can, throw your tsinelas, and outwit the taya.
description: A tactical take on the classic street game. Aim your throw, read the taya's patience, and time the dash to collect your slipper without getting tagged.
highlights: Physics-based throws with wind and slope
Short puzzle-like rounds you can finish on a break
Ranked ladder and local hot-seat mode

title: Barrio Tindahan
cultural_note: A sari-sari store is a small neighborhood shop that sells goods by the piece (tingi) and often on credit (utang). Many are run from the front of a family home.
short_description: Stock the shelves, sell by the piece, and keep your utang notebook honest.
description: Run a sari-sari store one day at a time. Sell tingi, order from the delivery truck, and decide whether to extend credit to the neighbour who is always a little short at the end of the month.
highlights: Hundreds of stocked items, from sachets to softdrinks in plastic
A neighbourhood that remembers how you treat people
Seasonal events from Undas to Noche Buena

title: Sigaw ng Bayan
cultural_note: The Katipunan was a secret society founded in 1892 to win independence from Spain. The 'Cry' of 1896 is traditionally taken as the start of the Philippine Revolution.
short_description: Organise secret meetings, pass coded messages, and build a movement without being caught.
description: A slow-burn strategy game set in 1896. Recruit across towns, manage trust and suspicion, and learn how real networks of people held together under surveillance.
highlights: Built with reference to published historical accounts
Message-passing puzzles with period ciphers
Codex entries that separate documented history from dramatisation

title: Jeepney Diaries
cultural_note: Jeepneys, first built from leftover US military jeeps, are one of the most iconic forms of public transport in the Philippines. Their bright paint and slogans make each one unique.
short_description: Drive your route, call out the stops, and pass the coins down the line.
description: Drive a jeepney from terminal to terminal. Pass fares along the bench, make change on the fly, and customise your ride with panels, stickers, and a very loud horn.
highlights: Relay fares hand to hand with 'bayad po'
Customisable body panels and paint
Routes inspired by real cities, with fictional street names

title: Kapre sa Balete
cultural_note: The kapre is a tall tree giant in Philippine folklore, said to live in old trees such as the balete and to smoke a large cigar. The smell of tobacco is the traditional sign of its presence.
short_description: The smell of tobacco is the first sign. The second is that the path behind you is gone.
description: A short, tense first-person horror about a night survey in an old balete grove. Navigate by smell and sound, share a light with the thing in the tree, and decide how much you owe it to leave.
highlights: Around two hours, designed for a single sitting
Audio-led horror: play best with headphones
Branching ending based on what you offer

title: Luksong Tinik
cultural_note: Luksong tinik ('jump over the thorns') is a traditional game where players leap over a barrier made from teammates' hands and feet, stacked higher each round.
short_description: The thorns keep stacking. Time your jump and clear the hands.
description: A one-button jumping game that grows from ankle-height to over your head. Tap to launch, hold to lengthen the arc, and keep the whole team in the game.
highlights: One-button rhythm jumping
Co-op mode where a missed jump costs the team
Plays well on low-end phones and laptops

title: Parol Makers
cultural_note: The parol is a star-shaped Christmas lantern traditionally made of bamboo and paper. San Fernando, Pampanga is famous for its giant lantern festival.
short_description: Cut bamboo, fold the paper, and wire the lights before Christmas Eve.
description: A relaxed crafting game about building parol for the neighbourhood. Fold, glue, wire, and hang your lanterns, then watch the street light up as other players' work joins yours.
highlights: Dozens of lantern frames and patterns
A shared street that fills with player creations
No timers, no fail states

title: Balangay Voyage
cultural_note: The balangay is an ancient plank-built wooden boat used for sea voyages and trade between islands. Surviving examples found in Butuan are more than a thousand years old.
short_description: Sail between islands, trade fairly, and keep your crew fed.
description: A voyage-planning strategy game across an archipelago. Read the winds and stars, carry goods that each island wants, and grow a trade network one landing at a time.
highlights: Star-and-wind navigation instead of a minimap
Barter economy with island-specific demand
Educator notes on the history behind each route

title: Bakunawa Eclipse
cultural_note: The Bakunawa is a giant serpent in Visayan mythology said to swallow the moon and cause eclipses. People once banged pots and pans to scare it away.
short_description: A dragon is eating the moon. Gather the village and make some noise.
description: An action RPG built around the story of the moon-eating dragon. Rally villagers, bang pots and pans to the rhythm, and chase the serpent across a sky that grows darker with every bite.
highlights: Rhythm-driven combat using everyday kitchen percussion
Village-building between eclipses
Original soundtrack with kulintang and gong ensembles
